transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19 16:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dana Liu (Blueframe Product), Ravi Patel (Blueframe SRE), Marta Gomez (Blueframe ML)

Summary: Quick demo of SDK wiring for function calls, review of early latency numbers from staging, discussion on structured output contract and who owns schema evolution. Lots of questions about KMS/VPC and where logs live.

Topics: SDK snippets, function calling, structured-output JSON schema, batching/kv cache, privacy/VPC

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — SDK function calling snippet review, results from the small latency run Marco did yesterday, and then get the schema ownership nailed down.
[00:22] Dana Liu: thanks Lena. high level we want to ensure the app-level invoke pattern is robust; our product team will own mapping user messages -> structured fields but want to make sure the model/SDK doesn't drift.
[00:35] Marco Ruiz: yep, i'll walk through the SDK example, then show the numbers. note the snippet uses the new invoke() helper, it wires up tools and function-calling in one shot.
[00:50] Ravi Patel: quick ask — network and KMS before we dive? our security folks want to know where the API keys live and if the kv cache touches PII.
[00:58] Lena Park: good call. short answer: hosted uses Redwood-managed KMS; Dedicated/Private can integrate with your KMS/HSM. Marco will point out where cache keys are ephemeral; by default we do prefix-only caching and don't persist raw prompts.
[01:18] Marco Ruiz: (shares screen) here is the SDK flow. you call redwood.sdk.invoke({prompt, tools, functions}) then the runtime will either stream tokens or return a function invocation structure. for structured output we recommend using the schema param so the runtime validates shape. code example shows function_name: 'extract_medical_entities' — returns JSON with fields: patient_id, findings, severity.
[01:40] Marta Gomez: small nit — in our data the patient_id is hashed on the client side; can we accept an opaque id type in the schema?
[01:47] Marco Ruiz: yes, schema types support string/opaque and you can attach a validation hook on the SE side. note: function-calling currently uses name-based routing; if you send two similar function names it may pick the closest.
[02:05] Dana Liu: are there any gotchas with function calling + streaming? we need partial updates to the UI while invocation runs.
[02:16] Marco Ruiz: streaming works fine; when the model decides to call a function the stream includes a function_call event. clients should buffer until function output completes. we also have an option to send function results back into the model as tool outputs for multi-step flows.
[02:36] Lena Park: Marco, show the latency run you mentioned.
[02:40] Marco Ruiz: right — i ran a small test from our staging fleet. workload: 500 requests, 8 concurrent, avg user message ~120 tokens, using a quantized open model pinned in staging. key numbers: median latency 210ms (token-first), p95 470ms. when we enable batching=auto and prefix cache on repeated prefixes p95 dropped to ~320ms.
[03:05] Ravi Patel: ok those numbers look promising. what was the kv cache size and eviction?
[03:12] Marco Ruiz: i used in-memory KV with a 10k entry cap and LRU eviction. important to note: prefix caching is keyed by reduced prompt fingerprint (not whole prompt) so we avoid storing PII. but if you run on-prem you can change retention policies.
[03:32] Marta Gomez: Marco, can you run the same test but with function-calling enabled? sometimes function dispatch adds 80-150ms.
[03:40] Marco Ruiz: sure, we saw a median bump of ~90ms in earlier tests. that was with synchronous function invocation where the runtime waits for the tool. if you use async function pattern (invoke tool separately) you can keep UI responsive and patch results later.
[03:58] Dana Liu: about schema evolution — who owns changes to the structured schema? product or ML? we want a clear workflow.
[04:08] Lena Park: good question. recommendation: product owns the canonical schema plus a versioned schema file in your repo, ML owns validation tests and a migration harness. Redwood can host a small webhook to validate outputs during CI if you want.
[04:26] Ravi Patel: security: where do logs go? and audit trails?
[04:30] Marco Ruiz: Hosted: logs stored in Redwood infra with retention configurable in tenant settings. Dedicated/private: logs can stay in your VPC or be pushed to your SIEM, and we support audit log forwarding. all logs can be configured to redact PII.
[04:47] Dana Liu: will we have to open ports for the private control plane? our infra needs specifics.
[04:52] Lena Park: for Private we use a control plane that talks over a fixed egress; most customers allow outbound TLS to our control plane endpoints. we'll share the network diagram.
[05:05] Marco Ruiz: back to SDK: i want to highlight a pattern — prefer explicit function calls with deterministic schema rather than free-text extraction for production. fewer hallucinations, easier regression testing.
[05:20] Marta Gomez: agreed. for ambiguous fields we can include a confidence score in the schema and a fallback route to human review.
[05:29] Marco Ruiz: yes, include confidence: { value: float, calibrated: boolean } — Redwood SDK can surface raw logits as well if you want to calibrate.
[05:42] Dana Liu: any notes about cost impact of batching vs low-latency? we need a guess for monthly costs if we enable aggressive caching.
[05:50] Marco Ruiz: aggressive caching and batching reduce token cost significantly but can increase memory/GPU usage. for your expected volume (~1.2M tokens/day) the estimate is ~20-30% reduction in token cost with prefix caching plus batching. we'll produce a spreadsheet with sensitivity.
[06:10] Ravi Patel: can we pin model versions to avoid behaviour changes during the POC?
[06:14] Lena Park: yes, you can pin model version in the route config. Redwood also supports canary rollouts — we can set traffic splits to 0.0/100.0 for testing.
[06:26] Marta Gomez: i have a practical question: when the model returns structured JSON it's sometimes slightly malformed from the model side — do you recommend post-parse validators?
[06:35] Marco Ruiz: absolutely. treat the model output as untrusted; run a JSON schema validator in the SDK client or a middleware. SDK has a validate(schema) call that enforces shape and can auto-retry with a different prompt templating.
[06:55] Dana Liu: can Redwood's SDK automatically re-prompt when validation fails? that might reduce engineering overhead.
[07:02] Marco Ruiz: yes, there's an optional "auto_repair" flag which will run up to N retries with a more constrained prompt and then surface a structured error if it still fails. cost impact is additive for retries.
[07:20] Lena Park: okay let's capture next steps — Marco will run additional tests including function-calling overhead and 1k/5k concurrency runs.
[07:28] Marco Ruiz: i'll do that, and i'll include both sync and async function flow numbers and the batching/prefix cache settings i used.
[07:33] Ravi Patel: i'll gather security questions, and invite our infra reviewer to next week's call.
[07:38] Marta Gomez: i'll prepare a sample set of anonymized messages and expected structured outputs — about 10k examples.
[07:44] Lena Park: i'll share the SDK snippet, the structured schema example, and a short how-to for wiring tools + function-calling.
[07:52] Dana Liu: perfect. anything else?
[07:55] Marco Ruiz: one more thing — some customers run a lightweight on-prem inference gateway for the KV cache to avoid egress; we can show an architecture diagram if you want.
[08:05] Ravi Patel: yes send the diagram.
[08:09] Lena Park: noted. we'll send resources after the call. thanks everyone — we'll reconvene next Tuesday same time.

(brief crosstalk, wrap up)

[55:30] End of meeting
